mcqs.q: Roughly what fraction of medical emergencies occur during dental procedures?
mcqs.explain: About half of all medical emergencies happen during dental procedures such as LA injection, extraction or pulp extirpation.

mcqs.q: Once cardiac arrest is recognised in the dental office, the immediate priority is to:
opts: Call EMS and start CAB (compressions, airway, breathing)
Sit the patient fully upright and wait
mcqs.explain: Call emergency medical services immediately and begin CAB; the rigid dental chair provides good support for chest compressions.

mcqs.q: Angina pectoris results from:
opts: An imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand
A bacterial infection of the valves
mcqs.explain: Angina is cardiac ischaemia caused by a mismatch between myocardial oxygen supply and demand.

mcqs.q: Which factor REDUCES myocardial oxygen supply?
mcqs.explain: Atherosclerosis, vasospasm and anaemia reduce supply; hyperthyroidism, hypertrophy and aortic stenosis increase demand.

mcqs.q: Which is a MODIFIABLE risk factor for coronary artery disease?
mcqs.explain: Modifiable factors include smoking, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension, diabetes, obesity and stress; age, male sex and family history are non-modifiable.

mcqs.q: The chest pain of angina characteristically radiates to the:
opts: Left arm, neck, jaw or teeth
mcqs.explain: Retrosternal anginal pain radiates to the left (± right) arm, neck, jaw, teeth or back — and can mimic dental pain in the mandible.

mcqs.q: Angina is classically precipitated by the '3 Es', which are:
mcqs.explain: The 3 Es are Exertion, Emotion and Eating; the pain is relieved by rest and nitrates.

mcqs.q: Stable angina is typically RELIEVED by:
mcqs.explain: Stable angina, lasting under 15 minutes, is relieved by rest and nitrates (GTN).

mcqs.q: The ECG during a stable-angina attack characteristically shows:
opts: ST elevation and pathological Q waves
mcqs.explain: Stable angina shows ST depression and T-inversion; ST elevation/pathological Q waves indicate myocardial infarction.

mcqs.q: A common and important side effect/interaction of GTN (glyceryl trinitrate) is:
opts: Throbbing headache and a dangerous interaction with sildenafil
mcqs.explain: GTN causes throbbing headache, flushing and dizziness, and dangerously potentiates sildenafil (severe hypotension).

mcqs.q: When angina does not respond to drug therapy, the next step is:
mcqs.explain: Refractory angina is treated by revascularization — percutaneous coronary intervention (balloon/stent) or coronary artery bypass grafting.

mcqs.q: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) includes:
mcqs.explain: ACS comprises unstable angina, non-ST-elevation MI (NSTEMI) and ST-elevation MI (STEMI).

mcqs.q: Myocardial infarction is confirmed by:
opts: Raised cardiac markers plus characteristic ECG changes
A normal ECG and normal troponin
mcqs.explain: MI is defined by elevated cardiac markers (troponin, CK-MB) together with ECG changes (ST elevation, T inversion, pathological Q waves).

mcqs.q: The most specific blood marker of myocardial damage is:
mcqs.explain: Troponin I and T are the most specific cardiac biomarkers; CK-MB and myoglobin are also used.

mcqs.q: How does the pain of myocardial infarction differ from angina?
opts: It is more severe, longer-lasting and NOT relieved by rest or sublingual nitrates
It is relieved instantly by GTN
mcqs.explain: MI pain is similar in site to angina but more severe, prolonged, and not relieved by rest or sublingual nitrates.

mcqs.q: For a STEMI, the key additional treatment is:
mcqs.explain: STEMI requires immediate reperfusion — thrombolytic therapy (streptokinase/alteplase) or primary PCI.

mcqs.q: The commonest cause of death after a myocardial infarction is:
mcqs.explain: Fatal arrhythmia is the most common cause of death after MI, so cardiac monitoring is essential.

mcqs.q: Why might anginal pain be mistaken for a dental problem?
opts: It can radiate to the mandible and mimic pain of dental origin
It always starts in the teeth
mcqs.explain: Angina radiating to the mandible can mimic dental pain, so a cardiac cause must be considered.

mcqs.q: Dental appointments for a patient with ischaemic heart disease are best scheduled as:
opts: Short, minimally stressful appointments in the late morning
Long sessions early in the morning
mcqs.explain: Short, minimally stressful late-morning appointments reduce stress-induced adrenaline release; early-morning and late-afternoon visits are avoided in IHD.

mcqs.q: Regarding epinephrine in local anaesthetic for a cardiac patient:
opts: Use a low concentration (≤1:100,000) with caution and slow injection
It is absolutely contraindicated in all cardiac patients
Inject it rapidly to finish quickly
mcqs.explain: Low-concentration epinephrine (≤1:100,000) may be used cautiously with slow injection; it is only rarely contraindicated (e.g. SBP >200/DBP >115).

mcqs.q: Elective dental surgery after a myocardial infarction should generally be deferred for:
mcqs.explain: Dental surgery within 6 months of an MI carries a high risk of re-infarction/arrhythmia, so elective procedures are deferred.

mcqs.q: If a patient develops chest pain during dental treatment, you should first:
opts: Stop treatment, sit them upright, and give sublingual GTN with oxygen
Lay them flat and continue working
mcqs.explain: Stop, keep the patient sitting upright, monitor vitals, and give sublingual GTN with oxygen, repeating every 5 minutes.

mcqs.q: Chest pain in the chair should be treated as a possible MI (chew 300 mg aspirin, call EMS) when it:
opts: Lasts more than 15–20 minutes or persists after 3 GTN doses
Improves on the first GTN dose
mcqs.explain: Suspect MI if pain is not relieved within 3 minutes, lasts >15–20 minutes, or persists after 3 GTN doses — give oxygen, 300 mg aspirin to chew and call EMS.

mcqs.q: Hypertension is defined as a persistent blood pressure of:
mcqs.explain: Hypertension is a persistent BP ≥140/90 mmHg (ESH); it affects 30–45% of adults.

mcqs.q: A characteristic feature of hypertension is that it:
opts: Usually has no warning signs or symptoms
Is easily seen on the face
mcqs.explain: Hypertension is usually symptomless ('silent') yet a major cause of premature death via MI, HF, CKD and stroke.

mcqs.q: The most common cause of SECONDARY hypertension is:
mcqs.explain: Renal causes account for over 80% of secondary hypertension; endocrine causes (phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's, acromegaly) are much rarer.

mcqs.q: When recording blood pressure, the systolic reading corresponds to:
opts: The pressure when the first tapping (Korotkoff) sounds appear
The pressure when the sounds disappear
mcqs.explain: Systolic = first appearance of Korotkoff sounds; diastolic = when the sounds become muffled and disappear.

mcqs.q: A patient in hypertensive crisis (SBP >180 or DBP >120 mmHg) during a dental visit should be:
opts: Have the procedure postponed and be referred to emergency care
mcqs.explain: In hypertensive crisis the dental procedure is postponed and the patient referred immediately to emergency care to prevent stroke/end-organ damage.

mcqs.q: Gingival hyperplasia (overgrowth) is an oral side effect of which antihypertensive?
mcqs.explain: Nifedipine and other calcium-channel blockers cause gingival hyperplasia; ACE-I cause dry cough/angioedema, beta-blockers/diuretics cause xerostomia and lichenoid reactions.

mcqs.q: NSAIDs should be avoided in a treated hypertensive patient because they:
mcqs.explain: NSAIDs (indomethacin, ibuprofen, naproxen) can antagonise antihypertensives and raise cardiovascular risk; paracetamol is preferred.

mcqs.q: The most common cause of heart failure is:
mcqs.explain: Ischaemic heart disease is the commonest cause; others include valvular disease, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, anaemia and thyroid disease.

mcqs.q: Which set of features points to RIGHT heart failure?
opts: Raised JVP, hepatomegaly, pitting leg oedema and ascites
Basal lung crackles and functional mitral regurgitation
mcqs.explain: Right HF causes systemic venous congestion — raised JVP, hepatomegaly, pitting leg oedema, ascites and pleural effusion; orthopnea/PND/crackles are features of left HF.

mcqs.q: For a patient with heart failure, dental management includes:
opts: Keeping the chair partially reclined/erect and avoiding GA until controlled
mcqs.explain: In HF keep the chair partially reclined/erect, delay elective care until controlled, and avoid GA (and NSAIDs/itraconazole) until the failure is stabilised.

saqs.q: Define angina, and list the factors that decrease supply and increase demand.
saqs.a: Cardiac ischaemia from an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand. Decreased supply: atherosclerosis, vasospasm, anaemia. Increased demand: hyperthyroidism, hypertrophy, aortic stenosis.

saqs.q: How is the pain of angina characterised (site, radiation, triggers, relief)?
saqs.a: Retrosternal tightness radiating to the left arm/neck/jaw/teeth, lasting <15 min, triggered by the 3 Es (exertion, emotion, eating) and relieved by rest and nitrates.

saqs.q: How does MI pain differ from angina, and how is STEMI treated?
saqs.a: MI pain is more severe, longer-lasting and NOT relieved by rest or nitrates. STEMI needs immediate reperfusion — thrombolysis (streptokinase/alteplase) or primary PCI — plus aspirin, oxygen, morphine and a β-blocker.

saqs.q: Outline the management of chest pain that develops during a dental procedure.
saqs.a: Stop treatment, sit the patient upright, give sublingual GTN + oxygen (repeat every 5 min). If pain lasts >15–20 min or persists after 3 doses → suspect MI: chew 300 mg aspirin and call EMS.

saqs.q: Define hypertension and give the ADA dental BP thresholds.
saqs.a: Persistent BP ≥140/90 mmHg. ADA: <160/100 → no modification; ≥160/100 → defer elective + physician consult; crisis >180/120 → postpone and refer to emergency (stroke risk).

saqs.q: List oral side effects of common antihypertensive drugs.
saqs.a: ACE-I: dry cough, ulcers, angioedema, taste loss. Beta-blockers/diuretics: xerostomia, lichenoid reactions. Calcium-channel blockers (nifedipine): gingival hyperplasia.

saqs.q: Contrast left and right heart failure, and state the dental precautions.
saqs.a: Left HF: exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, basal crackles. Right HF: raised JVP, hepatomegaly, pitting oedema, ascites. Dental: delay elective care until controlled, keep chair partially reclined/erect, avoid GA/NSAIDs.
